data.title: Major depressive disorder
data.summary: Explore Deep TMS when depression persists despite medication and other treatment.

image.alt: Person sitting by a bright window, looking out thoughtfully

data.detail_body:
Depression can affect motivation, sleep, appetite, concentration, and the ability to enjoy familiar activities. Major depressive disorder is a clinical diagnosis; symptoms and their impact should be assessed by a qualified professional.

When depression remains difficult after treatment, a clinician may discuss treatment-resistant depression and options beyond medication alone. UPTMS offers Deep TMS for major depressive disorder, with treatment selected after a review of your history and safety considerations.

A consultation is a chance to discuss which treatments you tried, how much they helped, and what you want to understand next. Insurance requirements are separate from the clinical decision.

data.title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
data.summary: Ask about Deep TMS for OCD and the evaluation needed to choose an appropriate protocol.

image.alt: Young man in rubber gloves scrubbing a table

data.detail_body:
OCD can involve distressing, unwanted thoughts and repetitive behaviors or mental rituals. Checking, washing, counting, and reassurance-seeking are examples; the condition can take forms that are not visible to other people.

The clinic’s dedicated OCD page describes BrainsWay Deep TMS using an H7 coil. The FDA-authorized OCD use is adjunctive treatment for adults, so discuss how it would fit alongside your current care rather than assuming it replaces medication or therapy.

Bring your treatment history, including any exposure and response prevention (ERP). Ask about the OCD-specific protocol and authorization criteria, which can differ from the depression pathway.

data.body:
Major depressive disorder can affect energy, concentration, sleep, and enjoyment—not just mood. It may become difficult to keep up with work, relationships, or the routines that used to feel familiar.

If antidepressants or therapy have not brought enough improvement, you may be searching for treatment-resistant depression options. A TMS consultation gives you space to review what you have tried and whether brain stimulation belongs in your care plan.

Our University Place clinic offers Deep TMS therapy for depression near Tacoma. Your provider considers your diagnosis, treatment history, medical needs, and goals before recommending a protocol.

image.alt: Patient on a sofa talking with a clinician who takes notes

data.answer: Bring a list of prior medications, how long you took them, any side effects, and the symptoms that still interfere with daily life. Ask what a TMS evaluation could clarify and how progress would be measured. This is a conversation guide, not a patient testimonial.

data.body:
Obsessive-compulsive disorder involves intrusive, unwanted thoughts and repetitive actions or mental rituals. It can include checking, contamination fears, counting, or repeated reassurance-seeking. OCD is more than liking things neat.

When symptoms remain difficult despite treatment, ask about Deep TMS for OCD in University Place. Our clinic’s OCD page describes a BrainsWay H7-coil protocol. Your clinician will explain how an OCD treatment plan differs from depression treatment.

Deep TMS is an adjunctive option for adults with OCD, meaning it can be part of a broader treatment plan. Discuss medication and exposure and response prevention (ERP) with your treating team; do not stop existing treatment on your own.

image.alt: Young woman with her hand at her chin, gazing out of a window

data.answer: You can start by describing how symptoms interrupt daily activities and what treatment you have already tried. You do not need to share every sensitive detail on an introductory call. Ask about an OCD-focused evaluation and coverage for that diagnosis.

data.body:
TMS stands for transcranial magnetic stimulation. It uses magnetic pulses to stimulate brain areas involved in mood regulation. Treatment takes place while you are awake, without surgery or anesthesia.

Our clinic uses BrainsWay Deep TMS technology. A provider reviews your treatment history and health needs before recommending whether it is an option for you.

faqs.question: What is TMS therapy?
faqs.answer: TMS uses magnetic pulses to stimulate targeted brain areas. It is an outpatient treatment that may be considered for depression when other treatments have not helped enough. [Read our TMS treatment guide.](/tms)

faqs.question: How do I know if TMS is right for me?
faqs.answer: A provider reviews your symptoms, past treatment, medical history, and safety considerations. Our free online self-assessment helps you prepare questions; it cannot diagnose a condition or determine eligibility.

faqs.question: Is the phone consultation free?
faqs.answer: Yes. The clinic offers a free initial phone consultation. Ask the team about charges for clinical evaluations and treatment, which are separate from that introductory call.

faqs.question: Will my insurance cover TMS?
faqs.answer: Coverage depends on your exact plan, diagnosis, treatment history, network status, and authorization requirements. Approval for depression does not automatically mean approval for OCD. Contact the clinic with the name of your plan to discuss what needs to be verified.

faqs.question: How many appointments will I need?
faqs.answer: TMS usually involves a series of visits over several weeks. Session length and frequency depend on your prescribed protocol. Your team will discuss the schedule before you decide to begin.

faqs.question: Are there side effects or reasons I cannot have TMS?
faqs.answer: Headache and scalp discomfort can occur. Seizures are a rare serious risk. Tell your provider about implants or metal near your head, seizure history, and medications so they can assess safety.

faqs.question: Should I stop my medication?
faqs.answer: Do not stop or change prescribed medication on your own. Discuss your current medications with your treating clinician and the TMS provider.

faqs.question: Can I contact you for a family member?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can call to ask general questions about care for a loved one. The clinic will explain patient consent and the evaluation steps needed to discuss individual care.

faqs.question: Are TMS and Deep TMS the same thing?
faqs.answer: TMS is the broader treatment category. Deep TMS is a type of TMS that uses a specialized coil design; UPTMS describes using BrainsWay technology. The prescribed device and protocol depend on the condition and clinical evaluation.

faqs.question: Does the same TMS protocol treat depression and OCD?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Depression and OCD treatment can involve different coils, stimulation targets, and session procedures. Tell the provider if you experience both so they can discuss an appropriate plan. [See the depression and OCD comparison.](/tms#treatment-differences)

faqs.question: Is Deep TMS for OCD FDA-cleared?
faqs.answer: The FDA authorized the BrainsWay Deep TMS system for OCD treatment in 2018. Its OCD indication is adjunctive treatment for adults. Device authorization does not determine whether a particular person is suitable or whether their insurance will cover treatment.

faqs.question: What is ERP, and is it relevant to OCD?
faqs.answer: Exposure and response prevention is a form of cognitive behavioral therapy used for OCD. It involves approaching triggers while learning to resist compulsions with professional guidance. Discuss ERP and medication history during your evaluation; listing this option does not mean UPTMS provides ERP therapy.

faqs.question: What does a TMS session feel like?
faqs.answer: You may hear clicking and feel tapping at the stimulation site. Scalp discomfort can occur. Ask about hearing protection, positioning, and how the team responds if you are uncomfortable.

faqs.question: How soon will I know whether treatment is helping?
faqs.answer: Improvement varies from person to person. Ask how symptoms will be assessed before, during, and after the course, and what the plan would be if progress is limited. No specific result or timeline can be promised.

faqs.question: How much does TMS treatment cost?
faqs.answer: Your cost depends on the prescribed course and your plan’s coverage, deductible, copay, or coinsurance. Ask for an estimate before treatment. The introductory phone consultation is free; clinical evaluations and treatment are separate.

faqs.question: Do I have to live in Tacoma to contact the clinic?
faqs.answer: No. The clinic is located in University Place and serves the Greater Tacoma area. Because treatment may require frequent visits, ask about appointment timing and travel before committing to a course.

conditions.title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
conditions.summary: Ask about Deep TMS for OCD and the evaluation needed to choose an appropriate protocol.

image.alt: Young man in rubber gloves scrubbing a table

conditions.detail_body:
OCD can involve distressing, unwanted thoughts and repetitive behaviors or mental rituals. Checking, washing, counting, and reassurance-seeking are examples; the condition can take forms that are not visible to other people.

The clinic’s dedicated OCD page describes BrainsWay Deep TMS using an H7 coil. The FDA-authorized OCD use is adjunctive treatment for adults, so discuss how it would fit alongside your current care rather than assuming it replaces medication or therapy.

Bring your treatment history, including any exposure and response prevention (ERP). Ask about the OCD-specific protocol and authorization criteria, which can differ from the depression pathway.

columns.title: When the focus is OCD

data.headline: Depression and OCD need their own treatment conversations.

data.body:
Before arranging treatment, consider travel from Tacoma or the surrounding area, work or caregiving commitments, and how repeated appointments would fit your week.

The clinic’s published guides describe an initial depression course of weekday visits over roughly four to six weeks and an OCD course that may span six to eight weeks. These are planning examples; your clinician must confirm the protocol and visit schedule recommended for you.

Session duration, total visits, and any continuation treatment depend on the prescribed protocol and your response. Ask for those details, plus expected costs, before beginning.

faqs.question: What does “treatment-resistant depression” mean?
faqs.answer: It describes depression that has not improved enough after appropriate treatment attempts. A clinician reviews which treatments were tried, at what dose, and for how long. An insurer may apply its own documentation criteria; a quiz cannot establish the diagnosis or authorize treatment.

faqs.question: Does having intrusive thoughts mean I have OCD?
faqs.answer: No single symptom establishes a diagnosis. A qualified mental health professional looks at the pattern, distress, compulsions, and impact on life, and considers other possible explanations. Seek an assessment rather than using this page to diagnose yourself.

faqs.question: What should I tell the provider about past treatment?
faqs.answer: Bring medication names, approximate dates, effects and side effects, therapy history, and any previous brain stimulation. For OCD, include any ERP experience. The clinic can explain how to share records through an appropriate channel.

faqs.question: What is the H7 coil mentioned on the OCD page?
faqs.answer: UPTMS identifies the H7 coil on its OCD service page. It is associated with the BrainsWay OCD treatment protocol. Ask the provider to explain the device and protocol planned for you, including how they differ from depression treatment.

faqs.question: What does “adjunctive OCD treatment” mean?
faqs.answer: Adjunctive means used as an addition to other care. BrainsWay’s OCD indication is adjunctive treatment for adults. Your treating team should explain how Deep TMS relates to your medication or psychotherapy plan.

faqs.question: Will an OCD session involve discussing symptom triggers?
faqs.answer: OCD protocols may include clinician-guided symptom provocation. Ask the provider whether that is part of the proposed protocol, what it involves, and how it will be supported. Do not attempt to create a treatment protocol from online instructions.

faqs.question: Can I compare results from different TMS studies?
faqs.answer: Only with context. Studies may involve different diagnoses, devices, protocols, and definitions of response or remission. A published percentage is not a prediction of your outcome or a verified success rate for this clinic.

faqs.question: What happens if treatment does not help enough?
faqs.answer: Ask in advance how response will be measured and when the provider will review the plan. Decisions about continuing, changing, or trying another treatment should be made with the treating clinician.

faqs.question: Can depression coverage be used to assume OCD coverage?
faqs.answer: No. Ask your insurer about coverage for the actual diagnosis and protocol being considered. Network status, prior authorization, and patient costs can differ, even under the same policy.

faqs.question: Is the self-check a clinical screening instrument?
faqs.answer: No. It is a short educational navigation tool created for this website. It does not calculate a validated symptom score, diagnose depression or OCD, or determine clinical or insurance eligibility. The clinic’s initial phone consultation is a separate next step.

data.title: What a Deep TMS session *feels like*
data.dek: A Deep TMS session is a short, seated outpatient visit. Here is what happens from check-in to the drive home, and what people commonly notice during the first week.

cover.alt: Patient seated under a TMS treatment helmet while a clinician looks on

content.text: Before the first session

Treatment starts only after a clinical evaluation. Your provider reviews your diagnosis, treatment history, medical needs and goals, and checks safety considerations such as metal near the head or a history of seizures.
At the first session the team measures the right position for the helmet and the right strength for you. This visit usually takes longer than the ones that follow.
During a session

You sit in a reclining chair and stay awake the whole time. A cushioned helmet rests on your head and delivers magnetic pulses. You will hear clicking and feel tapping on your scalp; earplugs are provided.
No anesthesia is needed.
You can talk with the technician between pulse trains.
Most sessions take about 20 minutes.
After a session
You can usually drive yourself home and return to your day. Some people notice headache or scalp discomfort in the first sessions; tell the team, because settings can often be adjusted.
Ask your provider how many sessions your course includes and how progress will be checked along the way.
For background on brain stimulation therapies, see the
National Institute of Mental Health
. To talk through your own situation,
request a free phone consultation
